claim: Gain-of-function mutations in the protein-tyrosine phosphatase SHP2 are the most frequently occurring mutations in sporadic juvenile myelomonocytic leukemia (JMML).
source: Gain-of-function mutations in the protein-tyrosine phosphatase SHP2 are the most frequently occurring mutations in sporadic juvenile myelomonocytic leukemia (JMML) and JMML-like myeloproliferative neoplasm (MPN) associated with Noonan syndrome (NS).
evidence: This claim is stated in the abstract and is supported by citations in the introduction section.

claim: Hematopoietic stem and progenitor cells (HSPCs) are the disease propagating cells of JMML.
source: Hematopoietic stem and progenitor cells (HSPCs) are the disease propagating cells of JMML.
evidence: This claim is stated in the abstract and is supported by citations in the discussion section.

claim: CRISPR/Cas9 knock-in Shp2D61G mutant zebrafish recapitulated a JMML-like MPN phenotype, including myeloid lineage hyperproliferation.
source: In addition to major NS traits, CRISPR/Cas9 knock-in Shp2D61G mutant zebrafish recapitulated a JMML-like MPN phenotype, including myeloid lineage hyperproliferation, ex vivo growth of myeloid colonies, and in vivo transplantability of HSPCs.
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data presented in Figure 2, showing increased numbers of neutrophils and macrophages in mutant zebrafish.

claim: CRISPR/Cas9 knock-in Shp2D61G mutant zebrafish showed ex vivo growth of myeloid colonies.
source: In addition to major NS traits, CRISPR/Cas9 knock-in Shp2D61G mutant zebrafish recapitulated a JMML-like MPN phenotype, including myeloid lineage hyperproliferation, ex vivo growth of myeloid colonies, and in vivo transplantability of HSPCs.
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data in Figure 2J and K showing colony-forming assays.

claim: CRISPR/Cas9 knock-in Shp2D61G mutant zebrafish showed in vivo transplantability of HSPCs.
source: In addition to major NS traits, CRISPR/Cas9 knock-in Shp2D61G mutant zebrafish recapitulated a JMML-like MPN phenotype, including myeloid lineage hyperproliferation, ex vivo growth of myeloid colonies, and in vivo transplantability of HSPCs.
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data in Figure 2L showing transplantation experiments.

claim: Single-cell mRNA sequencing of HSPCs from Shp2D61G zebrafish embryos and bulk sequencing of HSPCs from JMML patients revealed an overlapping inflammatory gene expression pattern.
source: Single-cell mRNA sequencing of HSPCs from Shp2D61G zebrafish embryos and bulk sequencing of HSPCs from JMML patients revealed an overlapping inflammatory gene expression pattern.
evidence: This claim is supported by data presented in Figures 4 and 5, showing inflammatory gene expression in both zebrafish and human samples.

claim: An anti-inflammatory agent rescued JMML-like MPN in Shp2D61G zebrafish embryos.
source: Strikingly, an anti-inflammatory agent rescued JMML-like MPN in Shp2D61G zebrafish embryos.
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data in Figure 6 showing dexamethasone treatment effects.

claim: A common inflammatory response was triggered in the HSPCs from sporadic JMML patients and syndromic NS zebrafish.
source: Our results indicate that a common inflammatory response was triggered in the HSPCs from sporadic JMML patients and syndromic NS zebrafish, which potentiated MPN and may represent a future target for JMML therapies.
evidence: This claim is supported by comparative transcriptomic analysis presented in Figures 4 and 5.

claim: 50% of NS patients carry heterozygous mutations in the protein-tyrosine phosphatase SHP2 (PTPN11).
source: NS is characterized by a systemic impact on development, most commonly resulting in short stature, congenital heart defects, and specific craniofacial characteristics (Rauen, 2013; Tajan et al., 2018).
evidence: This claim is stated in the introduction and is supported by citations.

claim: Somatic activating mutations in PTPN11 are the most common cause of sporadic juvenile myelomonocytic leukemia (JMML).
source: Somatic activating mutations in PTPN11 are the most common cause of sporadic juvenile myelomonocytic leukemia (JMML), a rare but aggressive myelodysplastic and myeloproliferative neoplasm (MPN) occurring in young children (Caye et al., 2015; Tartaglia et al., 2003).
evidence: This claim is stated in the introduction and is supported by citations.

claim: Children with NS are predisposed to developing neonatal MPN.
source: Consistently, children with NS are predisposed to developing neonatal MPN, that either regresses without treatment or rapidly progresses to JMML leading to early death (Kratz et al., 2005; Strullu et al., 2014).
evidence: This claim is stated in the introduction and is supported by citations.

claim: The D61G substitution in SHP2 is the most frequently occurring NS mutation associated with NS/JMML-like MPN.
source: The D61G substitution in SHP2 is the most frequently occurring (Strullu et al., 2014; Tartaglia et al., 2001).
evidence: This claim is stated in the results section and is supported by citations.

claim: The homology between human SHP2 and zebrafish Shp2a is 91%.
source: The homology between human SHP2 and zebrafish Shp2a is 91% and the amino acid D61 is located in an absolutely conserved region of the protein (Figure 1—figure supplement 1A).
evidence: This claim is supported by sequence alignment data shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 1A.

claim: The amino acid D61 is located in an absolutely conserved region of the protein.
source: The homology between human SHP2 and zebrafish Shp2a is 91% and the amino acid D61 is located in an absolutely conserved region of the protein (Figure 1—figure supplement 1A).
evidence: This claim is supported by sequence alignment data shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 1A.

claim: The introduced D61G mutation did not have a detectable effect on Shp2a protein expression.
source: Sequencing confirmed that the oligonucleotide used for the homology directed repair was incorporated correctly into the genome (Figure 1A) and that the introduced mutation did not have a detectable effect on Shp2a protein expression (Figure 1B).
evidence: This claim is supported by Western blot data shown in Figure 1B.

claim: In 32% of heterozygous Shp2D61G/wt zebrafish embryos at 5 days post fertilization, typical NS traits were observed.
source: Consistently, in 32% of heterozygous Shp2D61G/wt and 45% of homozygous Shp2D61G/D61G embryos at 5 days post fertilization (dpf) we observed typical NS traits, such as reduced body axis extension, heart edema, and craniofacial deformities.
evidence: This claim is supported by phenotypic analysis data shown in Figure 1C and D.

claim: In 45% of homozygous Shp2D61G/D61G zebrafish embryos at 5 days post fertilization, typical NS traits were observed.
source: Consistently, in 32% of heterozygous Shp2D61G/wt and 45% of homozygous Shp2D61G/D61G embryos at 5 days post fertilization (dpf) we observed typical NS traits, such as reduced body axis extension, heart edema, and craniofacial deformities.
evidence: This claim is supported by phenotypic analysis data shown in Figure 1C and D.

claim: The body axis length was significantly reduced in Shp2D61G mutant embryos at 5 dpf.
source: A more detailed characterization of the typical NS traits showed that the body axis length was significantly reduced in Shp2D61G mutant embryos at 5 dpf (Figure 1E).
evidence: This claim is supported by measurement data shown in Figure 1E.

claim: Imaging of Alcian blue-stained cartilage revealed NS-reminiscent craniofacial defects in 4 dpf Shp2D61G mutant embryos.
source: Furthermore, imaging of Alcian blue-stained cartilage revealed NS-reminiscent craniofacial defects in 4 dpf Shp2D61G mutant embryos, characterized by broadening of the head (Figure 1F), leading to an increased ratio of the width of the ceratohyal and the distance to Meckel's cartilage (Figure 1G).
evidence: This claim is supported by imaging data shown in Figure 1F and G.

claim: A decrease in heart rate was detected in Shp2D61G mutant hearts at 5 dpf.
source: A decrease in heart rate (Figure 1I), ejection fraction, and cardiac output (Figure 1—figure supplement 1D,E) was detected from the ventricular kymographs obtained from high-speed video recordings (Tessadori et al., 2012) of the Shp2D61G mutant hearts at 5 dpf (Figure 1H).
evidence: This claim is supported by heart rate measurement data shown in Figure 1I.

claim: A decrease in ejection fraction was detected in Shp2D61G mutant hearts at 5 dpf.
source: A decrease in heart rate (Figure 1I), ejection fraction, and cardiac output (Figure 1—figure supplement 1D,E) was detected from the ventricular kymographs obtained from high-speed video recordings (Tessadori et al., 2012) of the Shp2D61G mutant hearts at 5 dpf (Figure 1H).
evidence: This claim is supported by ejection fraction measurement data shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 1D.

claim: A decrease in cardiac output was detected in Shp2D61G mutant hearts at 5 dpf.
source: A decrease in heart rate (Figure 1I), ejection fraction, and cardiac output (Figure 1—figure supplement 1D,E) was detected from the ventricular kymographs obtained from high-speed video recordings (Tessadori et al., 2012) of the Shp2D61G mutant hearts at 5 dpf (Figure 1H).
evidence: This claim is supported by cardiac output measurement data shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 1E.

claim: The NS Shp2D61G mutant zebrafish phenocopied several of the typical NS traits, such as stunted growth, craniofacial defects, and heart defects.
source: Taken together, the NS Shp2D61G mutant zebrafish we established phenocopied several of the typical NS traits, such as stunted growth, craniofacial defects, and heart defects.
evidence: This claim is a summary of the phenotypic data presented in Figure 1.

claim: No effect of the Shp2D61G mutation on primitive hematopoiesis was observed in embryos at 2 dpf.
source: We were not able to observe any effect of the Shp2D61G mutation on primitive hematopoiesis in embryos at 2 dpf using WISH for markers of erythroid progenitors (gata-1), myeloid progenitors (pu.1), and white blood cells (l-plastin) (Figure 2—figure supplement 1A).
evidence: This claim is supported by WISH data shown in Figure 2—figure supplement 1A.

claim: A significant effect of the Shp2-D61G mutation on definitive hematopoiesis was observed at 5 dpf.
source: On the other hand, a significant effect of the Shp2-D61G mutation on definitive hematopoiesis was observed at 5 dpf (Figure 2).
evidence: This claim is supported by multiple experimental data shown in Figure 2.

claim: An increased number of CD41-GFPlow HSPCs was observed in the caudal hematopoietic tissue (CHT) region of the mutant embryos.
source: An increased number of CD41-GFPlow HSPCs was observed in the caudal hematopoietic tissue (CHT) region, corresponding to the fetal liver in human and the head kidney (corresponding to the bone marrow in human) of the mutant embryos (Figure 2A and B).
evidence: This claim is supported by confocal imaging and quantification data shown in Figure 2A and B.

claim: Shp2D61G mutation affects both proliferation and apoptosis of HSPCs.
source: Shp2D61G mutation seems to affect both proliferation and apoptosis of HSPCs, evident by an increase in CD41-GFPlow cells positive for phosphohistone H3 (pHis3), a marker for late G2 and M phase and a decrease in Acridine orange-positive cells in the CHT region, marking apoptotic cells (Figure 2—figure supplement 1B,C).
evidence: This claim is supported by immunohistochemistry and Acridine orange staining data shown in Figure 2—figure supplement 1B and C.

claim: An increase of c-myb-positive cells was observed in both CHT and head kidney region of the Shp2D61G mutants.
source: We observed an increase of c-myb-positive cells, marking HSPCs and of l-plastin-positive cells, marking all white blood cells, in both CHT and head kidney region of the Shp2D61G mutants (Figure 2C–F).
evidence: This claim is supported by WISH data shown in Figure 2C and D.

claim: An increase of l-plastin-positive cells was observed in both CHT and head kidney region of the Shp2D61G mutants.
source: We observed an increase of c-myb-positive cells, marking HSPCs and of l-plastin-positive cells, marking all white blood cells, in both CHT and head kidney region of the Shp2D61G mutants (Figure 2C–F).
evidence: This claim is supported by WISH data shown in Figure 2E and F.

claim: The size of the ikaros-positive thymus was not affected in Shp2D61G mutants.
source: These latter cells appear not to be lymphocytes, since the size of the ikaros-positive thymus was not affected (Figure 2—figure supplement 1D,E).
evidence: This claim is supported by WISH data shown in Figure 2—figure supplement 1D and E.

claim: The myeloid lineage was markedly expanded in Shp2D61G mutants, evident from the increase in the number of mpx-GFP-positive neutrophils.
source: On the other hand, the myeloid lineage was markedly expanded, evident from the increase in the number of mpx-GFP-positive neutrophils (Figure 2G and H) and mpeg-mCherry-positive macrophages (Figure 2G1), in Tg(mpx:GFP, mpeg:mCherry) double transgenic mutant embryos.
evidence: This claim is supported by confocal imaging and quantification data shown in Figure 2G and H.

claim: The myeloid lineage was markedly expanded in Shp2D61G mutants, evident from the increase in the number of mpeg-mCherry-positive macrophages.
source: On the other hand, the myeloid lineage was markedly expanded, evident from the increase in the number of mpx-GFP-positive neutrophils (Figure 2G and H) and mpeg-mCherry-positive macrophages (Figure 2G1), in Tg(mpx:GFP, mpeg:mCherry) double transgenic mutant embryos.
evidence: This claim is supported by confocal imaging and quantification data shown in Figure 2G and I.

claim: Shp2D61G mutant embryos displayed a mild decrease in the number of CD41-GFPhigh-positive thrombocytes.
source: Shp2D61G mutant embryos also displayed a mild decrease in the number of CD41-GFPhigh-positive thrombocytes and the number of β-globin-positive erythrocytes (Figure 2—figure supplement 1F-H).
evidence: This claim is supported by quantification data shown in Figure 2—figure supplement 1F.

claim: Shp2D61G mutant embryos displayed a mild decrease in the number of β-globin-positive erythrocytes.
source: Shp2D61G mutant embryos also displayed a mild decrease in the number of CD41-GFPhigh-positive thrombocytes and the number of β-globin-positive erythrocytes (Figure 2—figure supplement 1F-H).
evidence: This claim is supported by WISH data shown in Figure 2—figure supplement 1G and H.

claim: The observed defects in all different blood lineages examined were stronger in the homozygous Shp2D61G/D61G than heterozygous Shp2D61G/wt embryos, supporting a dosage effect.
source: The observed defects in all different blood lineages examined here were stronger in the homozygous Shp2D61G/D61G than heterozygous Shp2D61G/wt embryos, supporting a dosage effect.
evidence: This claim is supported by comparative data across genotypes shown in Figure 2.

claim: Colonies developed from the CD41-GFPlow cells isolated from the Shp2D61G/wt zebrafish embryos at 5 dpf and exposed to Gcsfa were larger in size and number compared to their wild type siblings.
source: Compared to their wild type (wt) siblings, colonies developed from the CD41-GFPlow cells isolated from the Shp2D61G/wt zebrafish embryos at 5 dpf and exposed to Gcsfa were larger in size and number, demonstrating an enhanced CFU-G and CFU-M colony-forming ability (Figure 2J and K).
evidence: This claim is supported by colony-forming assay data shown in Figure 2J and K.

claim: Animals injected with mutant WKM cells accumulated GFP- and mCherry-positive cells near the site of injection starting at 14 days and increasing until 28 days.
source: Animals injected with 1 × 105 mutant WKM cells (3/5) accumulated GFP- and mCherry-positive cells near the site of injection starting at 14 days and increasing until 28 days.
evidence: This claim is supported by transplantation experiment data shown in Figure 2L.

claim: Animals injected with WKM cells from control sibling animals with wt Shp2a lacked any GFP- and mCherry-positive cells.
source: By contrast, animals injected with WKM cells from control sibling animals with wt Shp2a (5/5) lacked any GFP- and mCherry-positive cells (Figure 2L).
evidence: This claim is supported by transplantation experiment data shown in Figure 2L.

claim: The Shp2D61G mutant zebrafish embryos develop multilineage hematopoietic defects during the definitive wave of fetal hematopoiesis, which originates in the HSPCs compartment.
source: Our findings suggest that the Shp2D61G mutant zebrafish embryos develop multilineage hematopoietic defects during the definitive wave of fetal hematopoiesis, which originates in the HSPCs compartment.
evidence: This claim is a summary of the hematopoietic defect data presented in Figure 2.

claim: The observed defect in Shp2D61G zebrafish is reminiscent of JMML-like MPN in human NS patients.
source: The observed defect is reminiscent of JMML-like MPN in human NS patients.
evidence: This claim is an inference based on the similarity of phenotypes between zebrafish and human patients.

claim: Four major clusters were identified in the single-cell RNA sequencing analysis of CD41-GFPlow cells.
source: Clusters were visualized by t-distributed stochastic neighbor embedding (t-SNE) and four major clusters were further analyzed (Figure 3C).
evidence: This claim is supported by single-cell RNA sequencing data shown in Figure 3C.

claim: Cluster 1 cells were determined to be thrombocyte and erythroid progenitors.
source: Based on the differentially expressed genes (DEGs) and GO term analysis, cells from Cluster 1 were determined to be thrombocyte and erythroid progenitors, cluster 2 hematopoietic stem cell (HSC)-like HSPCs, cluster 3 early myeloid progenitors, and cluster 4 monocyte/macrophage progenitors (Figure 3C, Figure 3—figure supplement 1A, Supplementary file 1).
evidence: This claim is supported by differential gene expression analysis and GO term analysis shown in Figure 3C and Figure 3—figure supplement 1A.

claim: Cluster 2 cells were determined to be hematopoietic stem cell (HSC)-like HSPCs.
source: Based on the differentially expressed genes (DEGs) and GO term analysis, cells from Cluster 1 were determined to be thrombocyte and erythroid progenitors, cluster 2 hematopoietic stem cell (HSC)-like HSPCs, cluster 3 early myeloid progenitors, and cluster 4 monocyte/macrophage progenitors (Figure 3C, Figure 3—figure supplement 1A, Supplementary file 1).
evidence: This claim is supported by differential gene expression analysis and GO term analysis shown in Figure 3C and Figure 3—figure supplement 1A.

claim: Cluster 3 cells were determined to be early myeloid progenitors.
source: Based on the differentially expressed genes (DEGs) and GO term analysis, cells from Cluster 1 were determined to be thrombocyte and erythroid progenitors, cluster 2 hematopoietic stem cell (HSC)-like HSPCs, cluster 3 early myeloid progenitors, and cluster 4 monocyte/macrophage progenitors (Figure 3C, Figure 3—figure supplement 1A, Supplementary file 1).
evidence: This claim is supported by differential gene expression analysis and GO term analysis shown in Figure 3C and Figure 3—figure supplement 1A.

claim: Cluster 4 cells were determined to be monocyte/macrophage progenitors.
source: Based on the differentially expressed genes (DEGs) and GO term analysis, cells from Cluster 1 were determined to be thrombocyte and erythroid progenitors, cluster 2 hematopoietic stem cell (HSC)-like HSPCs, cluster 3 early myeloid progenitors, and cluster 4 monocyte/macrophage progenitors (Figure 3C, Figure 3—figure supplement 1A, Supplementary file 1).
evidence: This claim is supported by differential gene expression analysis and GO term analysis shown in Figure 3C and Figure 3—figure supplement 1A.

claim: An overrepresentation of mutant Shp2D61G/wt and Shp2D61G/D61G cells was observed in the HSC-like HSPCs cluster.
source: An overrepresentation of mutant Shp2D61G/wt and Shp2D61G/D61G cells was observed in the HSC-like HSPCs cluster and monocytes/macrophages progenitors cluster, whereas these were underrepresented in the thrombocyte and erythroid progenitors cluster (Figure 3D and E).
evidence: This claim is supported by single-cell RNA sequencing data shown in Figure 3D and E.

claim: An overrepresentation of mutant Shp2D61G/wt and Shp2D61G/D61G cells was observed in the monocytes/macrophages progenitors cluster.
source: An overrepresentation of mutant Shp2D61G/wt and Shp2D61G/D61G cells was observed in the HSC-like HSPCs cluster and monocytes/macrophages progenitors cluster, whereas these were underrepresented in the thrombocyte and erythroid progenitors cluster (Figure 3D and E).
evidence: This claim is supported by single-cell RNA sequencing data shown in Figure 3D and E.

claim: Mutant Shp2D61G/wt and Shp2D61G/D61G cells were underrepresented in the thrombocyte and erythroid progenitors cluster.
source: An overrepresentation of mutant Shp2D61G/wt and Shp2D61G/D61G cells was observed in the HSC-like HSPCs cluster and monocytes/macrophages progenitors cluster, whereas these were underrepresented in the thrombocyte and erythroid progenitors cluster (Figure 3D and E).
evidence: This claim is supported by single-cell RNA sequencing data shown in Figure 3D and E.

claim: An increased number of pu.1-positive cells was detected by WISH in 5 dpf old Shp2D61G embryos compared to their Shp2wt siblings.
source: An increased number of pu.1-positive cells was detected by WISH in 5 dpf old Shp2D61G embryos compared to their Shp2wt siblings (Figure 3G and H), whereas the number of alas2-positive cells in Shp2D61G mutants was decreased (Figure 3J and K).
evidence: This claim is supported by WISH data shown in Figure 3G and H.

claim: The number of alas2-positive cells in Shp2D61G mutants was decreased.
source: An increased number of pu.1-positive cells was detected by WISH in 5 dpf old Shp2D61G embryos compared to their Shp2wt siblings (Figure 3G and H), whereas the number of alas2-positive cells in Shp2D61G mutants was decreased (Figure 3J and K).
evidence: This claim is supported by WISH data shown in Figure 3J and K.

claim: Single-cell RNA sequencing suggests that defects during early differentiation of HSPCs to monocyte/macrophage progenitors and erythroid/thrombocyte progenitors initiate the multilineage blood defect observed in Shp2D61G embryos.
source: Taken together, single-cell RNA sequencing suggests that defects during early differentiation of HSPCs to monocyte/macrophage progenitors and erythroid/thrombocyte progenitors initiate the multilineage blood defect observed in Shp2D61G embryos, which recapitulates features of NS-JMML-like MPN.
evidence: This claim is a summary of the single-cell RNA sequencing data presented in Figure 3.

claim: Functional annotation of the DEGs and the GO term enrichment analysis revealed enhanced expression of proinflammatory genes in mutant Shp2D61G cells in the monocyte/macrophage progenitors cluster.
source: Functional annotation of the DEGs and the GO term enrichment analysis revealed enhanced expression of proinflammatory genes in mutant Shp2D61G cells (Figure 4A and B, Supplementary file 1).
evidence: This claim is supported by differential gene expression analysis and GO term analysis shown in Figure 4A and B.

claim: Expression of inflammation-related genes, such as gcsfa, gcsfb, il1b, irg1, and nfkbiaa, was constrained to the cells of mutant Shp2D61G genotype in the monocyte/macrophage progenitors cluster.
source: Interestingly, expression of inflammation-related genes, such as gcsfa, gcsfb, il1b, irg1, and nfkbiaa, was constrained to the cells of mutant Shp2D61G genotype in the monocyte/macrophage progenitors cluster, whereas the monocyte marker timp2b was equally expressed by cells of distinct genotypes (Figure 4B).
evidence: This claim is supported by single-cell RNA sequencing data shown in Figure 4B.

claim: The monocyte marker timp2b was equally expressed by cells of distinct genotypes in the monocyte/macrophage progenitors cluster.
source: Interestingly, expression of inflammation-related genes, such as gcsfa, gcsfb, il1b, irg1, and nfkbiaa, was constrained to the cells of mutant Shp2D61G genotype in the monocyte/macrophage progenitors cluster, whereas the monocyte marker timp2b was equally expressed by cells of distinct genotypes (Figure 4B).
evidence: This claim is supported by single-cell RNA sequencing data shown in Figure 4B.

claim: Expression of the monocyte marker timp2b started during early differentiation of monocyte/macrophage progenitors.
source: Expression of the monocyte marker timp2b started during early differentiation of monocyte/macrophage progenitors. The level of timp2b expression was similar in Shp2wt and Shp2D61G HSPCs.
evidence: This claim is supported by pseudotime analysis shown in Figure 4E.

claim: The level of timp2b expression was similar in Shp2wt and Shp2D61G HSPCs.
source: Expression of the monocyte marker timp2b started during early differentiation of monocyte/macrophage progenitors. The level of timp2b expression was similar in Shp2wt and Shp2D61G HSPCs.
evidence: This claim is supported by pseudotime analysis shown in Figure 4E.

claim: Expression of the inflammatory genes, il1b, gcsfa, irg1, nfkbiaa, and tnfa, started at a similar pseudotime as timp2b expression, but with a more robust expression in Shp2D61G HSPCs than in Shp2wt HSPCs.
source: Expression of the inflammatory genes, il1b, gcsfa, irg1, nfkbiaa, and tnfa, started at a similar pseudotime as timp2b expression, but with a more robust expression in Shp2D61G HSPCs than in Shp2wt HSPCs.
evidence: This claim is supported by pseudotime analysis shown in Figure 4E.

claim: High expression of IL-1β was validated in mutant Tg(il1b:eGFP, mpeg:mCherry) transgenic embryos in vivo.
source: Finally, high expression of IL-1β was validated in mutant Tg(il1b:eGFP, mpeg:mCherry) transgenic embryos in vivo. IL-1β-eGFP-positive cells were more abundant in the CHT region of Shp2D61G embryos than in wt embryos (Figure 4F).
evidence: This claim is supported by in vivo imaging data shown in Figure 4F.

claim: IL-1β-eGFP-positive cells were more abundant in the CHT region of Shp2D61G embryos than in wt embryos.
source: Finally, high expression of IL-1β was validated in mutant Tg(il1b:eGFP, mpeg:mCherry) transgenic embryos in vivo. IL-1β-eGFP-positive cells were more abundant in the CHT region of Shp2D61G embryos than in wt embryos (Figure 4F).
evidence: This claim is supported by in vivo imaging data shown in Figure 4F.

claim: Shp2D61G embryos display proinflammatory gene expression in HSPCs, which is initiated during early differentiation of the monocyte/macrophage progenitor cells.
source: Taken together, Shp2D61G embryos display proinflammatory gene expression in HSPCs, which is initiated during early differentiation of the monocyte/macrophage progenitor cells.
evidence: This claim is a summary of the inflammatory gene expression data presented in Figure 4.

claim: 1478 DEGs were identified in HSPCs from JMML patients, compared to the healthy donor HSPCs.
source: Overall, we identified 1478 DEGs in HSPCs from JMML patients, compared to the healthy donor HSPCs (Figure 5A, Supplementary file 3).
evidence: This claim is supported by differential gene expression analysis shown in Figure 5A.

claim: Altered expression of genes related to inflammation was the most prominent in JMML HSPCs, such as genes involved in TNFα signaling via NFκB.
source: Strikingly, altered expression of genes related to inflammation was the most prominent, such as genes involved in TNFα signaling via NFκB.
evidence: This claim is supported by GSEA analysis shown in Figure 5B.

claim: The inflammatory response genes were significantly enriched in JMML HSPCs.
source: The inflammatory response genes were significantly enriched in JMML HSPCs (Figure 5B–D).
evidence: This claim is supported by GSEA analysis shown in Figure 5B-D.

claim: De-regulation of genes related to proliferation (G2M checkpoint, MYC targets, and E2F targets) was evident in JMML HSPCs, suggesting their decreased quiescence.
source: De-regulation of genes related to proliferation (G2M checkpoint, MYC targets, and E2F targets) was evident in JMML HSPCs, suggesting their decreased quiescence (Figure 5B).
evidence: This claim is supported by GSEA analysis shown in Figure 5B.

claim: GSEA revealed that human orthologs of the top 100 DEGs found in the zebrafish monocyte/macrophage progenitor cells were enriched significantly in patient JMML HSPCs.
source: GSEA revealed that human orthologs of the top 100 DEGs found in the zebrafish monocyte/macrophage progenitor cells were enriched significantly in patient JMML HSPCs (Figure 5E).
evidence: This claim is supported by GSEA analysis shown in Figure 5E.

claim: Some of the top overexpressed inflammation-associated genes in JMML patients, such as TNF and MARCKSL, were also overexpressed in NS/JMML-like MPN mutant zebrafish embryos compared to the wt.
source: Some of the top overexpressed inflammation-associated genes in JMML patients, such as TNF and MARCKSL, were also overexpressed in NS/JMML-like MPN mutant zebrafish embryos compared to the wt (Figure 5F and G).
evidence: This claim is supported by gene expression comparison data shown in Figure 5F and G.

claim: Zebrafish signature genes were able to clearly segregate HSPCs from JMML patients and healthy donors in 3D principal component analysis.
source: 3D principal component analysis (PCA) visualized that these zebrafish signature genes were able to clearly segregate HSPCs from JMML patients and healthy donors (Figure 5H).
evidence: This claim is supported by PCA analysis shown in Figure 5H.

claim: Mutant, activated SHP2 triggers proinflammatory gene expression in HSPCs both in sporadic JMML patients and in the zebrafish model of syndromic JMML-like MPN in a similar manner, suggesting a common underlying, endogenously driven process.
source: These findings suggest that mutant, activated SHP2 triggers proinflammatory gene expression in HSPCs both in sporadic JMML patients and in our zebrafish model of syndromic JMML-like MPN in a similar manner, suggesting a common underlying, endogenously driven process.
evidence: This claim is a summary of the comparative transcriptomic analysis presented in Figure 5.

claim: Both CI1040 and LY294002 led to a robust reduction in expansion of both HSPCs and myeloid lineage in mutant embryos.
source: Both CI1040 and LY294002 led to a robust reduction in expansion of both HSPCs and myeloid lineage in mutant embryos, measured by WISH using markers for c-myb and l-plastin (Figure 6B and C), demonstrating that the NS-associated blood development defect in Shp2D61G embryos was largely caused by overactivation of the RAS-MAPK and PI3K pathways as expected.
evidence: This claim is supported by inhibitor treatment data shown in Figure 6B and C.

claim: The NS-associated blood development defect in Shp2D61G embryos was largely caused by overactivation of the RAS-MAPK and PI3K pathways.
source: Both CI1040 and LY294002 led to a robust reduction in expansion of both HSPCs and myeloid lineage in mutant embryos, measured by WISH using markers for c-myb and l-plastin (Figure 6B and C), demonstrating that the NS-associated blood development defect in Shp2D61G embryos was largely caused by overactivation of the RAS-MAPK and PI3K pathways as expected.
evidence: This claim is supported by inhibitor treatment data shown in Figure 6B and C.

claim: Dexamethasone reduced c-myb and l-plastin expression to a similar extent as CI1040 and LY294002.
source: To our surprise, dexamethasone reduced c-myb and l-plastin expression to a similar extent as CI1040 and LY294002 (Figure 6B and C), indicating a profound role for the inflammatory response in the pathogenesis of NS-associated blood defects.
evidence: This claim is supported by inhibitor treatment data shown in Figure 6B and C.

claim: The inflammatory response has a profound role in the pathogenesis of NS-associated blood defects.
source: To our surprise, dexamethasone reduced c-myb and l-plastin expression to a similar extent as CI1040 and LY294002 (Figure 6B and C), indicating a profound role for the inflammatory response in the pathogenesis of NS-associated blood defects.
evidence: This claim is inferred from the dexamethasone treatment data shown in Figure 6B and C.

claim: Upon dexamethasone treatment, the number of mpx-GFP and mpeg-mCherry-positive cells decreased in Shp2D61G embryos to similar levels as observed in Shp2wt embryos.
source: Upon dexamethasone treatment, the number of mpx-GFP and mpeg-mCherry-positive cells decreased in Shp2D61G embryos to similar levels as observed in Shp2wt embryos, indicating that dexamethasone treatment rescued the expansion of the myeloid lineage in Shp2D61G embryos.
evidence: This claim is supported by dexamethasone treatment data shown in Figure 6D-F.
